messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo, a 28-year-old prison guard, described his life as having been split in two. There was the "before," a time he remembered with a hazy sense of warmth, and the "after," the last eight months of grinding, gray existence. The event that cleaved his life was the rainy Tuesday night he was driving his younger brother, Javier, home from a concert. One moment they were laughing, the radio loud, and the next, there was the sickening screech of tires on wet asphalt as another car ran a red light. Mateo remembers the feeling of the world tilting, the horrifying crunch of metal, and then a profound, floating sense of unreality as he looked over and saw Javier. That feeling of detachment, of watching a terrible movie he couldn't stop, was the first thing to haunt him.

In the weeks that followed, Mateo found that the world was filled with landmines. A news report on a local traffic accident would send a jolt through him, and he would have to cover his face with his hands, pressing his palms into his eyes to block out the image of the mangled cars. His wife, Sofia, would try to talk about her day, and if a coworker's family troubles involved illness or loss, Mateo would feel an internal switch flip. The conversation became a direct commentary on his own failure. These moments would trigger an immediate, crushing certainty: he should have protected Javier. He had been the older brother, the one driving, the one in charge, and he had failed. To escape the thought, he would retreat into himself, making it clear through his silence that the topic was closed, effectively avoiding any reminder of his grief.

This sense of personal failure began to metastasize, poisoning his view of himself and his future. He came to believe he was fundamentally broken, that the happy, easygoing man he used to be was gone forever, replaced by someone miserable. This conviction that he had no future made him hyper-attuned to any hint of loss, creating a state of constant, low-grade threat monitoring. A casual mention of a funeral by one of the other guards at the prison felt like a personal accusation, a fresh piece of evidence confirming his status as a failure. It was during his shifts that the most unsettling trigger emerged: that sense of detachment he first felt in the wreck. During a tense lockdown or a chaotic cell search, the world would suddenly seem muffled and distant, as if he were watching it on a screen. This feeling of unreality was terrifying because it was a direct echo of the crash, and it would instantly activate the searing thought, "I failed to protect him."

The weight of these beliefs—that he was a failure, that he had no future, that he was doomed to be miserable—became unbearable. He found that the only way to silence the internal accusations was with external noise. He started picking arguments with Sofia over nothing, escalating minor disagreements into shouting matches. In the heat of the conflict, the raw adrenaline of anger would temporarily drown out the guilt and the terrifying sense of detachment. He did the same at work, interpreting ambiguous comments from inmates as direct challenges, seeking the physical confrontation that would ground him in the present. But the relief was fleeting. The aftermath of these conflicts only served to reinforce his darkest appraisals of himself. After a fight, seeing Sofia’s hurt and exhausted face, he would be filled with a fresh wave of self-loathing. "I used to be a happy person," he thought, "but now I am always miserable. I'm destroying everything." The tense silence in their apartment after an argument became its own trigger, a quiet space that screamed of loss and confirmed his hopelessness.

Mateo sought therapy after Sofia told him she couldn't live like this anymore. The thought of losing her, of failing to protect another person he loved, was paralyzing. He feels trapped in a vicious cycle he cannot escape. The strategies he uses to survive the moments of intense distress—the avoidance, the conflict—are the very things cementing his belief that he is a lost cause, a man with no future. He is terrified of the dissociative feelings, certain they are a sign he is losing his mind, and even more terrified that the misery he now radiates will eventually drive everyone he loves away, leaving him utterly alone with his failure.
